title: The Big Lie Of Childhood Trauma
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses how to handle the unpredictable disruptions every school day brings -- fire alarms, outages, schedule changes -- by advocating for a habit of deliberate 'professional distance' from both students and situations outside a teacher's control. He argues that a teacher's visible stress directly worsens student behavior in the moment, so the real skill is stepping back into a broader, calmer vantage point rather than reacting from inside the narrow, anxious frame of the disruption. This professional distance is built the same way as other SCM habits: relying on the classroom management plan, following through calmly, and starting each day with brief morning visualization, practiced daily until it becomes an automatic disposition rather than a forced effort. The payoff, in his framing, is that unexpected events stop derailing the day and instead barely register, letting a teacher redirect students and move on without losing momentum.
points: Maintaining 'professional distance' from students, the job, and situations outside your control is presented as the core skill for handling sudden disruptions.
A teacher's own visible stress and anxiety during an unexpected event directly worsens how students behave in that moment.
Professional distance is built through daily practice, especially morning visualization, until it becomes a default disposition rather than effortful self-control.
With practice, unexpected disruptions stop derailing an entire day and become minor, quickly-resolved interruptions instead.
quotes: Events and incidents out of your control invade your well-ordered peace like the hordes of Cimbri.
Your present mood and disposition also transfer to your students. The more anxious and frustrated you feel, the worse they’ll behave.
Here at SCM we’ve long promoted the benefits of maintaining a professional distance—from students, from the job, and from situations out of your control.
For those who practice the discipline of never getting too invested or deep in the emotive weeds, unexpected events act as a trigger to draw back, run cooler, and breathe deeper.
Yes, the unexpected will still strike at the worst possible time. But it will no longer ruin the moment, let alone your whole day.
